# Applications: a data maturity assessment and roadmap (Indianapolis Colts, business side)

Note: this talk covers commercial and business data (ticketing, sponsorship, marketing), not athlete data. Applications below are about method and organization, not metrics.

## Where this applies

- Inference: Run a short maturity self-assessment of Applied Performance, using the talk's structure: a few capability areas, each scored from awareness through leading [04:42], with a target level for two years out set by stakeholders [06:45]. Areas could be data collection, storage, analysis, reporting and decision use, which map to Eric's existing gap list.
- Inference: Interview the coaches and staff who consume reports (position coaches, Athletic Medicine, Athletic Performance) the way the Colts interviewed 24 staff [05:43], and ask what level of capability they need within two years. The talk found friction came from people, process and unclear goals, not only technology [06:13].
- Inference: Turn the gap list into a mapped set of initiatives, where each initiative is tied to several capabilities (strategy, process, organization, technology, KPIs [10:19]) and sequenced, with the foundation item first (their warehouse was placed first [11:50]). For Baylor, the foundation item might be a single athlete table that links GPS, force plate, PFF and roster data.
- Inference: Start a recurring cross-unit data meeting like their weekly "center of excellence" [24:09], with analysts from Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition and Athletic Performance, to share projects and avoid silo work.
- Inference: Before buying or building a data layer, write down what the layer must do (break silos, scale, speed up insight, allow collaboration [13:53]) and judge options against that list.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: his Development Plan runs a gap analysis (no intern curriculum, no sport-specific data dictionaries, no operational checklists, no Baylor-specific technology workflows, no guiding-principles framework) and sets a three-phase roadmap (Foundation, Operational Depth, Education and Culture). The talk agrees in method: assess, find gaps, build a phased blueprint (about two and a half years [07:47]).
- Eric's baseline: Kitman Labs is the cross-technology data store and visualization layer, distinct from each vendor's reporting tool. The talk extends this: the Colts moved from an out-of-box product to a customized, internally owned warehouse and said this may not suit other organizations [13:23]. No stated conflict; Eric's view on build versus buy is not in the baseline.
- Eric's baseline: the data dictionary is organized by vendor rather than by sport, which he flags as a usability problem. The talk's point that the schema should fit the organization's needs rather than the reverse [19:30] is consistent with this.
- Eric's baseline: Performance Team Collaboration is one of four operating principles. The talk agrees and extends it with a concrete structure (liaison staff per department plus a weekly forum [24:41]).
- Eric's baseline: standardized coach-facing reporting templates do not yet exist. The talk's argument that self-serve tools reduce analyst bottlenecks [15:54] bears on that gap.

## What would have to be true

- Stakeholders will answer a maturity questionnaire honestly, and the scoring scale has to be defined in advance so results can be compared a year later. The talk shows only a single total score and does not give the scale details beyond five levels and 10 capabilities.
- Someone owns follow-through. The Colts cite ownership-level commitment [25:53]; at Baylor the equivalent would be support from the Applied Performance and sport leadership.
- A real integration need exists (the same athlete appearing in several systems with different IDs) before investing in a warehouse.

## Do not apply when

- The decision is about athlete training or health metrics. This is a business-side talk with no athlete data, so nothing here validates a monitoring method.
- Staff time is too short to run a 24-person interview round; shrink it rather than adopt the full process.
- Copying the Colts' stack. The speaker says a custom build might not be right for others [13:23], and the talk was presented under Sigma sponsorship and names vendors (Snowflake, Data Climber as captioned) as chosen partners, not as tested recommendations.
- Treating the 62 out of 100 score as a benchmark. It is the Colts' own internal score on their own scale [08:17].

## First step

Draft a one-page list of five Applied Performance capability areas, score each as aware, developing, practicing, optimizing or leading, and share it with one staff member for disagreement. Nothing is built or bought.

# Applications: biomechanics and consistency in basketball shooting

## Where this applies

- Inference: Treat consistency, not peak output, as the metric of interest for closed, repeatable skills. For Baylor football this points to kickers and punters (the same motion every attempt), where rep-to-rep variability in force plate or video measures could be tracked alongside outcome. The talk argues the best free throw shooters are the most consistent across timing and joint angles [14:48].
- Inference: In VALD ForceDecks work, report the spread of repeated trials (for example CMJ trials for the same athlete) next to the average, since the talk's central evidence is a composite of repeated attempts (20 free throws overlaid [13:17]). The spread is a cheap consistency measure from data Baylor already collects.
- Inference: Read a failure as symptom versus cause. The speaker says arm inconsistency in long shots may be a symptom of energy not coming up from the ground [19:54], which is his belief and not shown. A parallel use at Baylor is checking whether an upper-body outcome problem (for example throwing or blocking) has a lower-body or trunk contributor, before changing the upper-body drill.
- Inference: For basketball (if Applied Performance supports it), sample athletes across several days and states before reading a biomechanical profile, since the speaker agrees one capture day may reflect soreness or injury [21:59].
- Inference: Use the "MRI, not surgery" role split: Applied Performance supplies the measurement and the coach decides the correction [23:00]. This fits how Eric would hand findings to a position coach.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: testing protocols have to be repeatable ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April") or the data cannot be compared. The talk agrees and extends it: it applies repeatability to the athlete's own movement, not only to the test procedure.
- Eric's baseline: metric selection follows a framework of output, driver and strategy metrics (adopted from Hawkin Dynamics). The talk's idea that outcome (the miss), driver (joint velocity) and where in the sequence the error arises [12:14] reads as similar in structure. This is an inference, not something the speaker said.
- Eric's baseline: "Favor a small number of valid, reliable tests." The talk conflicts in spirit for its own method: 25 joints at 250 times a second with many derived metrics [13:47], which the speaker calls a curation problem.
- Eric's baseline: "do not reassess an athlete if there is known fatigue" and a trained "coach's eye" matters as much as technology. The talk agrees: capture days can be unrepresentative [21:59], and the coach is the conduit for correction [23:00].
- Eric's baseline: Performance Team Collaboration is a core principle. The talk agrees: its conclusion is that analyst, biomechanist and coach must be integrated [20:26].

## What would have to be true

- The measure has to be tied to an outcome that matters (for example kick distance or accuracy), shown with enough athletes. The talk shows composites for two or three shooters only, with no group statistics.
- Repeated trials per athlete under similar conditions, and a sampling plan across weeks.
- A way to capture movement that athletes tolerate. The talk calls the marker suit intrusive and not fun [09:10]; Baylor's available tools (force plates, video) are less invasive but less precise.
- A person who can act on a finding (a coach willing to try the change).

## Do not apply when

- The skill is open and reactive (tackling, route running). The speaker himself says contextual shots such as step-backs differ from the closed free throw [08:09].
- Only one capture day exists for an athlete who may be sore or injured [21:59].
- Using his basketball numbers. The velocity tolerance (about 0.4 to 0.5 mph [11:14]) and the missed-three pattern [10:43] are for shooting and do not transfer to other skills.
- Treating "consistency is good" as proven. The speaker cites literature and examples, and agrees on Q&A that every athlete has a different form [24:03]; the talk gives no sample sizes.
- Presuming the speaker's collaboration or lab is neutral: he is an ESPN analyst promoting a partnership with Mint Athletic Performance (caption spelling).

## First step

Take one repeated-trial dataset Baylor already has (for example CMJ trials for a position group), compute each athlete's trial-to-trial spread for a single metric, and see whether the spread differs between athletes. No change to testing is needed.

- Using his basketball numbers. The velocity tolerance (about 0.4 to 0.5 mph [11:14]) and the missed-three pattern [10:43] are for shooting and do not transfer to other skills.
- Treating "consistency is good" as proven. The speaker cites literature and examples, and agrees on Q&A that every athlete has a different form [24:03]; the talk gives no sample sizes.
- Presuming the speaker's collaboration or lab is neutral: he is an ESPN analyst promoting a partnership with Mint Athletic Performance (caption spelling).

## First step

Take one repeated-trial dataset Baylor already has (for example CMJ trials for a position group), compute each athlete's trial-to-trial spread for a single metric, and see whether the spread differs between athletes. No change to testing is needed.

=== FILE: videos/2022-03-25_Rn7sZ5kNsNw_using-technology-to-monitor-workload-in-elite-figure-skating/summary.md ===
---
type: video-summary
video_id: Rn7sZ5kNsNw
title: "SSAC22: Using Technology to Monitor Workload in Elite Figure Skating"
event: SSAC22 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Lindsey Slater (caption spelling: "lindsey slater")]
topics: [sports-science, injury-health, other-sport:figure-skating]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

The speaker, a physical therapy professor and the sport science manager for U.S. Figure Skating, describes replacing pen-and-paper jump logs with a single hip-worn motion sensor. The first goal was to count training workload, with performance and technique feedback second, because elite athletes reject being told what to do. Three case studies show the sensor used to guide a return after puberty, to set a daily jump limit, and to test whether a skater could realistically land a triple axel by a deadline. The talk matters for athlete monitoring because it ties a device output to individual rep limits, and it shows that adoption depended on who drove the project.

## Key claims

- Vertical loading on a pop jump was found to match that of triple and quad jumps, so early monitoring counted every jump equally [01:32].
- Self-logged jump counts were unreliable: athletes skipped pop jumps and counted combinations as one [02:34].
- Priority one was tracking workload, not judging performance; telling an Olympic athlete what to do risks losing them [03:06].
- A four-sensor setup was first tested on one top athlete, and the speaker says no earlier system had captured the rotation of a triple lutz without saturating [04:38].
- Sensors on the full ice surface avoided the marker-system limit of jumping inside one circle [05:08].
- A single sensor on the hip, smaller than a smartwatch, gives immediate app feedback on jump type, revolutions, rotation speed, air time, height and timing of peak angular velocity; some outputs are estimates and loop jumps are hardest [06:40], [07:10], [07:41].
- Case 1 (post-puberty return): triple axel work was paused, rotation rose over months, peaked around May, dipped in July after a vaccination, and recovered by August [09:44], [10:16], [10:46].
- Time to peak rotation moved earlier toward a point just over halfway through the jump as she improved [11:16].
- The second jump in a combination shows angular velocity like a triple axel, so it carries heavy rotational landing load; coaches were told to track triple-triples with triple axels and quads [12:18], [12:48].
- After tracking those together, the athlete had no further hip pain flare-ups [13:50].
- Case 2: the athlete underestimated her daily jumps; rotation fell across a two-hour session, and the concern was residual fatigue the next day [14:20], [14:51].
- A 75-jump daily ceiling was set, with two recovery days required if she chose to exceed it; the ceiling was raised after progressive exposure with no fatigue [15:23], [15:54], [16:24].
- Case 3: after about four months of data the team judged a triple axel by the target date unrealistic because her rotation appeared capped at the triple; she returned the sensor [17:25], [18:25].
- Adoption pattern: coach-driven succeeded, athlete-driven succeeded, practitioner-driven did not [18:55], [19:26].
- The work was funded by the USOPC and developed with the sensor company in about a year [19:57], [20:58].

## Numbers and definitions

- Triple axel rotation needed for a woman: about 1900 to 1950 degrees per second; the speaker estimates the Russians at 2000 to 2100 (estimate) [09:14].
- Case 1 athlete rotated about 1750 degrees per second on return in February; reached the 1900s in March [09:14], [10:16].
- Setup time: about 5 minutes for sensors versus an hour or more for markers; 11 sensors about 10 minutes versus 30 to 45 minutes for a marker system [05:08], [06:09].
- Case 2: thought she did 60 to 70 jumps a day; actual close to 100 [14:20]. Limit 75; beyond it, two days around 40 jumps [15:23], [15:54]. Later limit 85 (caption is garbled around "high low days are 85") [16:24].
- Five of the six single skaters at the games wore the sensor [08:13].
- Residual fatigue: still fatigued the next day [14:51].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Wearable IMU (single hip sensor, plus a four-sensor and an 11-sensor test) with app-based jump detection and an algorithm refined with more data [07:41].
- Peak angular velocity and time to peak, combined, as the two key measures [18:25].
- Individual thresholds and a progressive increase in allowed volume, compared by the speaker to progressive overload [15:54].
- Comparison of one athlete's trend against athletes who can land triple axels [17:55].

## Limits and open questions

- Three case studies, no group statistics, no accuracy figures against video.
- The speaker says the old jump-height finding (doubles versus triples) probably needs retesting with today's quads [02:03].
- Internal tension: the talk begins with "all jumps are equal" and later says not all jumps are equal [01:32], [13:19].
- The "no flare-ups" result is one athlete without a control [13:50].
- The ceiling-effect judgement in Case 3 is the speaker's belief; the athlete rejected it [17:25].
- The speaker is the sport science manager for the governing body, with an institutional interest.
- Caption problems: sensor company transcribed as "40 motion sports" and "4d sports"/"4d motion" [04:08], [06:40], [20:58]; "cheetah jump" [07:10] is probably garbled; "pear skaters" is pairs [26:18].

## Q&A

- Spins: not measured; loading is jump based; a boot sensor is planned for the next phase [22:06].
- Arms overhead: has data but keeps it private; the speaker says it reduces inertia and helps young skaters but is harder after puberty [23:10], [23:40], [24:10].
- Baseball pitch counts and volleyball jump counts are being explored with a single sensor [24:45], [25:16].
- Pairs skating: hip sensor is not workable, other locations are being discussed [26:18].

=== FILE: videos/2022-03-25_VZEYQU2-Oc8_how-data-journey-started-for-the-indianapolis-colts/summary.md ===
---
type: video-summary
video_id: VZEYQU2-Oc8
title: "SSAC22: How Data Journey Started for the Indianapolis Colts"
event: SSAC22 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Charlie Shin (caption spelling: "charlie shin")]
topics: [front-office, decision-making, american-football]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

The Colts' vice president of data strategy and analytics describes how the club started a data program on the business side (ticketing, sponsorship, marketing), not on-field analytics. The team scored itself on a five-level maturity scale across five areas, interviewed staff, set two-year targets, and built a roadmap of initiatives, with a custom cloud data warehouse first. The speaker argues that technology alone does not fix data problems, and that people, process and clear goals matter as much. The Q&A covers team structure, a cross-department forum, and gaining leadership buy-in. The talk is useful as a method for assessing and sequencing data work, with no athlete data shown.

## Key claims

- The club began from its mission, then asked which capabilities to build or improve, with limited money and people [02:05], [02:37], [03:09].
- Having technology does not help without the right people to use it [03:09].
- A data maturity framework covered five areas (customer strategy, infrastructure, analytics, operations, performance tracking), each scored from awareness through leading [04:11], [04:42], [05:12].
- Interviews showed friction came from people, process and unclear goals, not only technology [06:13].
- Stakeholders were asked where capability needed to be in two years, which produced the gap [06:45], [07:15].
- The main infrastructure need was an integrated view of fans across touch points, not "a data warehouse" as such [10:19], [10:50].
- Designing the warehouse is partly art, since the schema must reflect strategy and use [11:20].
- The warehouse was sequenced as an immediate item because it enabled others [11:50].
- The club moved from an out-of-box solution to a custom one, and says this may not suit other organizations [12:53], [13:23].
- Four selection considerations: break silos, scale without third parties, faster insight, collaboration through self-serve tools [13:53], [14:24], [15:24], [15:54].
- Delivery: an outside firm (caption: "data climber") built it and handed over full ownership; Snowflake is the cloud warehouse; master data management gives a single view [17:57], [18:29], [19:00].
- Benefits claimed: customizable, IP owned, schema built for their needs, less duplication, speed and cost control [19:30], [20:01].
- The journey is described as never ending [20:31].

## Numbers and definitions

- 24 staff interviewed across commercial departments, finance, executives and ownership [05:43].
- Five strategic areas, two components each, so 10 capabilities; five maturity levels (awareness to leading) [04:42], [08:17].
- Score of 62 out of 100 on the internal assessment [08:17].
- Blueprint spanning about two and a half years [07:47]; stakeholders were asked about two years out [06:45].
- 12 initiatives in the roadmap [11:50].
- "Center of excellence" meets weekly [24:41].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Data maturity framework with questionnaires and qualitative interviews [05:12], [06:13].
- Gap analysis (current versus target level) turned into programs and initiatives mapped to capabilities, tagged to strategy, process, organization, technology and KPIs [07:47], [09:49], [10:19].
- Roadmap with layers and timelines, warehouse first [11:50].
- Matrix of staff skills (strategy and analytics, CRM and platforms, activation of data) tied to vertical departments, plus a cross-department center of excellence [22:05], [23:07], [24:09].

## Limits and open questions

- Business-side data only; no athlete, performance or injury content.
- Results of the program are not reported; the work was in progress at the time [20:31].
- The speaker says he cannot share all the initiatives [09:19]; the scoring scale and per-area scores are not shown in the captions.
- 62 out of 100 is an internal measure with no external benchmark; the answer about outside-industry benchmarking gives no numbers [30:29].
- The talk was presented under a sponsor (Sigma, per the host introduction) and names vendors chosen by the club, which is institutional and commercial context [00:01].
- Caption problems: "data climber", "snowflakes", "russell scabetti" and "tan" (probably the team) may be misspelled [15:54], [18:29], [29:28].

## Q&A

- Team structure: three staff with distinct skill sets, each tied to a department, plus a weekly center of excellence [22:05], [24:09].
- Second question: the audience question is garbled; the answer covers ownership's commitment, treating the group as an internal service, and building buy-in over time [25:53], [26:24], [26:55].
- Benchmarking: teams share practices through a league community call (caption: "russell scabetti"); the club also looks outside sports for ideas [29:28], [29:58], [30:29].

=== FILE: videos/2022-03-25_mtdVRx3t1eo_the-biomechanics-of-buckets-the-next-revolution-in-basketbal/summary.md ===
---
type: video-summary
video_id: mtdVRx3t1eo
title: "SSAC22: The Biomechanics Of Buckets: The Next Revolution In Basketball Analytics"
event: SSAC22 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Kirk Goldsberry (caption spelling: "kurt goldsberry")]
topics: [basketball, sports-science, competitive-advantage]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

An ESPN analyst describes an early-stage project to apply 3D motion capture to basketball shooting, aiming to explain why some shooters miss more than others. He argues analytics is moving from outcomes to processes and from game data to practice and lab data. His main finding so far is that struggling free throw shooters show more joint-to-joint inconsistency than strong ones, particularly at the shoulder, elbow and wrist. He treats free throws as the easiest case and expects "shooting labs" to follow the pitching labs in baseball. He closes by saying the winners will integrate biomechanists, analysts and coaches.

## Key claims

- Three shifts in analytics: outcomes to processes, game data to game plus practice and lab data, and measurement moving toward player development rather than surveillance [02:32], [03:02], [03:32], [04:03].
- Goal: a "shot chart for the human body," asking why some shooters are better than others [06:06], [06:37].
- Free throws are a closed, repeatable task and the lowest hanging fruit; threes are contextual and harder [07:37], [08:09], [08:39].
- Current accurate biomechanics requires a marker suit and many cameras, which is intrusive; he hopes for a markerless future [08:39], [09:10], [09:41].
- Most missed NBA threes in the ring data are short or long, not left or right [10:43].
- Good free throw shooters control ball velocity; the tolerance for error is small [11:14].
- He describes Giannis Antetokounmpo's typical free throw miss as short, which he reads as a velocity deficit with a consistent arc [11:44].
- Velocity errors in launch trace to the shoulder, elbow and wrist; weaker free throw shooters are less consistent in angles and timing [14:17], [14:48], [15:21].
- Long threes are growing, and biomechanics could explain why some shooters can extend range and others cannot [17:54], [18:24].
- A shooting coach cited a "tight body, tight ball" idea about core strength for deep range [18:54].
- His own hypothesis: arm inconsistency on deep shots is a symptom, with energy leaking from the ground and trunk as the cause; he says he is still working on it [19:54].
- Prediction: biomechanists will sit in every NBA basketball operations group, and teams that integrate biomechanics, analytics and coaching will gain an advantage [20:26], [20:56].

## Numbers and definitions

- 40 cameras in the motion capture array [08:39].
- About 800,000 missed threes plotted from second-tracking ring data since 2013 (the speaker says "or something") [10:12].
- Velocity tolerance of about four tenths to half a mile per hour, depending on the shot [11:14].
- One struggling free throw shooter: 20 free throws overlaid, 54 percent; a shooter at 85 or 90 percent shown as a comparison [13:17], [14:48].
- Capture: 25 joints, 250 times a second, sub-millimeter accuracy [13:47].
- An NBA three-point shooter at 40 percent from a 24-foot shot shown with consistent mechanics [18:24].

## Methods and frameworks named

- 3D marker-based motion capture with a compression suit, with derived metrics per shot [08:39], [13:47].
- Composite overlays of repeated shots to show joint consistency at each phase [13:17], [14:48].
- Motor control framing of closed versus open tasks [07:37].
- Kinematic sequence and phases (base, flow and energy transfer, launch) to locate sources of error [12:14], [18:54], [19:54].
- Collaboration with a biomechanist and an Austin company (caption: "mint athletic performance"), working with a few NBA teams [10:12], [12:45].

## Limits and open questions

- Early stage: the speaker says the project is "just starting"; no sample size, number of players or outcome study is given.
- Evidence shown is composite images of a few shooters, with 54 percent and 85 to 90 percent as single-player examples.
- The speaker is not a biomechanist [09:41] and calls the "symptom versus cause" idea a belief [19:54].
- Capture sessions may not represent a typical day, and his sampling strategy is not defined [21:59].
- The ESPN analyst and collaboration partners have a commercial interest in the proposed future.
- Caption spellings to check: "kurt goldsberry", "kate/k jackson", "mint", "phil beckner", "rachel marty from noaa" [06:37], [10:12], [18:54].

## Q&A

- Day-to-day or week-to-week consistency and streakiness: plausible, but he has no answer; needs a sampling strategy across time [21:59].
- Next step after finding an inconsistency: a shooting coach, likened to treatment after an MRI; his role is identifying the problem [23:00], [23:32].
- Whether form matters less than consistency: every shooter has an individual kinematic strategy and consistency within it is key [24:03].
- Link between body size and consistency: no data yet; mechanics change through development, and this method could track that [25:06].

Caption problems: the sensor company in the skating talk (transcribed "40 motion sports"/"4d sports"/"4d motion"), the Colts vendor and community-call names, and the basketball names listed above; skating Case 2 limit "85" is garbled at [16:24]; the Colts audience question at [25:53] is garbled. I could not verify the "high low days are 85" meaning or the Colts' scale details.
